U-3 vs. U-6 Unemployment Rate: An Overview

The U-3 unemployment rate, or U3 rate, is the most commonly reported rate of unemployment in the United States and represents the number of people actively seeking a job. The U-6 rate, or U6, includes discouraged, underemployed, and unemployed workers in the country.1﻿

U-3 is the rate of unemployment released each month by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), but many economists view the U-6 rate as the more meaningful rate because it covers a larger percentage of people who are unemployed.2

﻿

Along with the economic growth rate and the inflation rate, the unemployment rate is one of the most widely reported and discussed economic indicators. It is regularly cited in the news because it provides a simple snapshot of the condition of the economy. Many assume that the unemployment rate is a straightforward measure of people who are out of work, but the reality is more complicated.

U-6 Unemployment Rate

Unlike the U-3 rate, the U-6 unemployment rate includes a whole swath of unemployed people—namely, everyone not listed in the U-3 rate. That means the U-6 rate is much truer to a natural, non-technical understanding of what it means to be unemployed.1﻿

This rate accounts for anyone who has been seeking employment for at least 12 months but left discouraged without being able to secure a job. It also includes anyone who has gone back to school, become disabled, and people who are underemployed or working part-time hours.1﻿

By capturing everyone who exists on the margins of the labor market, the U-6 rate provides a broad picture of the underutilization of labor in the country. In this sense, the U-6 rate may be considered the true unemployment rate.

At the end of April 2020, for example, in the midst of the pandemic, the U-3 unemployment rate was 14.7%, while the U-6 rate was 22.8%
